title: Castle to Safety
subtitle: Tuck the king away before the fight begins.
goals: Recognize when one side is unsafe
Choose king safety over pawn grabs

steps.say: Learn to castle to safety. A king in the center is a target on an open board — one tactic away from disaster. Castling solves two problems at once: the king gets a pawn shield, and a rook wakes up.

steps.prompt: Your kingside pieces are developed and the path is clear. Castle!
hints: King two squares toward the h1 rook — both pieces move in one turn.
Tap the king, then the g1 square.

line.say: Safe! The king hides behind f2, g2, h2, and the rook eyes the center files. Now the real fight can begin on your terms.

rejections.say: Nxe5! The c6 knight recaptures and you've traded a developed knight for one pawn — with your king still in the middle. Safety first, snacks later.
A one-piece attack with an uncastled king — Black defends f7 easily and your knight gets pushed around. Castle first, attack second.

steps.wrongSay: Everything is ready — this is the moment to castle kingside.
steps.successSay: Develop, castle, THEN attack — the professional move order.

steps.prompt: White has castled — don't fall behind. You're Black: castle too!
hints: Your kingside is clear: bishop and knight are both developed.
King to g8, rook to f8 — one move.

line.say: Level again — both kings are safe, both h-rooks awake. Castling isn't just for White!

rejections.say: dxe4! The e4 pawn was guarded by d3 — you lost a whole knight grabbing it, with your king still in the center. Castle first; count pawns later.
That rook shuffle throws away your castling rights forever — the one move that did the same job better WAS castling.

steps.wrongSay: Match White's king safety — castle kingside now.
steps.successSay: When both sides castle early, the game is decided by skill — not by cheap central ambushes.

steps.prompt: You want to castle — but look closely at g1. Kingside is poisoned! Castle the OTHER way.
hints: The c5 bishop stares straight through the open f2 hole at g1 — the king may not castle INTO check.
Your queenside is clear: b1, c1, d1 are all empty. Go long!

line.say: Castled long! The king ducks to c1 — away from that laser bishop — and your rook lands on the d-file instantly. When one wing is compromised, use the other.

rejections.say: The king shuffles sideways, loses castling forever, and buries the h1 rook. Queenside castling was legal and solved everything in one move.
Into the center?! The king blocks his own pieces and stands in the crossfire. Castle long — b1, c1 and d1 are clear.

steps.wrongSay: Kingside castling is illegal here — the c5 bishop covers g1. But the queenside is wide open...
steps.successSay: Two castling options means a flexible king. Always check BOTH wings.

steps.prompt: A pawn seems free, an attack looks tempting — but what does the position really demand?
hints: Ask the three opening questions: Are my pieces out? Is my king safe? THEN can I attack?
Minor pieces developed: check. King safety: not yet. That's your answer.

line.say: The disciplined move. The e5 'free' pawn was defended, the knight raid premature — castling completes your setup and threatens nothing less than a perfect game.

rejections.say: Nxe5! It was never free — the c6 knight guards it. You gave a knight for a pawn because the king rush blurred your counting.
The knight attacks f7 — but Black castles or plays d5 and your 'attack' evaporates, leaving a misplaced knight. One-piece attacks fail against decent defense.
A do-nothing move while your king stands in the center. If you can't find a developing move, castling is almost always right.

steps.wrongSay: Pieces developed, king in the center — the position is begging for one particular move.
steps.successSay: Develop, castle, connect the rooks. Master that rhythm and you're never worse out of the opening.
